sentences.text: Adult Thescelosaurus measured approximately 3 to 4 meters in length and weighed between 200 and 300 kilograms.
This bipedal dinosaur had a long tail that made up half its body length and was stiffened by ossified tendons.
It possessed a long, low snout ending in a toothless beak.
Thescelosaurus possessed more teeth than related genera, and these teeth varied in type.
A near-complete skeleton was discovered in July 1891 by John Bell Hatcher and William H. Utterback along Doegie Creek in Niobrara County, Wyoming.
The genus was named and described in 1913 by the paleontologist Charles W. Gilmore.
Gilmore published the preliminary description of the species Thescelosaurus neglectus in 1913.
Later, the species T. garbanii was named in 1976 and T. assiniboiensis was named in 2011.
Thescelosaurus was an herbivore that likely fed selectively, based on its teeth and narrow snout.
It had robust limbs with a femur longer than its tibia, suggesting it was not adapted for running.
The dinosaur had a comparatively small brain, which may indicate it lived in small groups of two to three individuals.
Thescelosaurus had acute senses of smell and balance but poor hearing.
Thescelosaurus is the namesake genus of the family Thescelosauridae.
Bugenasaura is a synonym of the genus Thescelosaurus.
Thescelosaurus edmontonensis was named by Sternberg in 1940 but is considered a nomen dubium.
Thescelosaurids are classified either as basal ornithopods or as a group outside ornithopods within Neornithischia.
Thescelosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous period, specifically the late Maastrichtian age.
It lived until around 66 million years ago, shortly before the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event.
Fossils of Thescelosaurus have been found across a wide range in western North America.
Scientists now doubt the identification of a fossilized heart in a Thescelosaurus specimen that was unearthed in 1999.
William J. Morris argued that the ankle anatomy and larger size of a specimen were unique, leading him to name the new species T. garbanii.
William J. Morris suggested that T. edmontonensis and T. garbanii might eventually be separated from Thescelosaurus as a new genus.
It is debated whether the hindlimb of T. garbanii actually belongs to the pachycephalosaurid Stygimoloch.
